reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Glioblastoma is the most common and most aggressive primary malignant brain tumour in adults, classified as a grade 4 glioma
Presentation is usually subacute over weeks, with progressive headache, focal deficits, cognitive or personality change, and seizures
Headaches suggesting raised intracranial pressure, worse in the morning or with Valsalva, and new focal neurology should prompt urgent imaging
On MRI it typically appears as an irregularly enhancing mass with central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic oedema, often crossing the corpus callosum as a butterfly lesion
Definitive diagnosis and molecular characterisation require tissue from biopsy or resection, with markers such as IDH status and MGMT promoter methylation guiding prognosis and therapy
Corticosteroids are used to control symptomatic peritumoural oedema and mass effect while treatment is planned
Standard management combines maximal safe surgical resection with subsequent radiotherapy and chemotherapy, individualised to patient fitness and molecular profile
Despite multimodal treatment the tumour almost always recurs, so realistic goal-setting and supportive care are integral
reference.pathophysiology: Glioblastoma is a highly malignant, infiltrative tumour arising from glial (astrocytic-lineage) cells. It is characterised histologically by marked cellular atypia, brisk mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and regions of necrosis. The tumour cells invade diffusely along white matter tracts well beyond the enhancing margin seen on imaging, which underlies the difficulty of complete removal and the near-inevitable recurrence. Aberrant angiogenesis produces leaky vessels that generate surrounding vasogenic oedema and contribute to mass effect and raised intracranial pressure. Distinct molecular alterations define subgroups with differing behaviour and treatment response.
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain with contrast, including advanced sequences (perfusion, spectroscopy) to characterise the lesion
Histopathological and molecular analysis of biopsy or resection tissue (including IDH and MGMT status)
Staging or systemic imaging when metastasis is a differential
Assessment of performance status and comorbidity to guide treatment intensity
redFlags: Rapidly progressive neurological deficit or declining consciousness from mass effect
Symptoms and signs of raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation
Acute deterioration from intratumoural haemorrhage or worsening oedema
reference.prognosis: Glioblastoma carries a poor prognosis with median survival typically measured in months to a couple of years even with optimal multimodal therapy; younger age, good performance status, greater extent of resection, and favourable molecular markers such as MGMT methylation are associated with better outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming a solitary enhancing lesion is glioblastoma without considering metastasis, lymphoma, or abscess
Starting high-dose steroids before biopsy when lymphoma is a possibility, as this can obscure the diagnosis
Underestimating infiltration beyond the enhancing margin when planning treatment
Neglecting seizure control, symptom management, and early supportive care discussions
management: Maximal safe surgical resection to reduce tumour burden and obtain tissue for histological and molecular diagnosis
Adjuvant fractionated radiotherapy with concurrent and maintenance temozolomide chemotherapy as standard combined-modality treatment
Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone to control symptomatic peritumoural vasogenic oedema and mass effect
Antiepileptic drugs for seizure control and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis given the prothrombotic risk
Use MGMT promoter methylation and IDH status to guide therapy, and consider tumour-treating fields or bevacizumab for progressive or recurrent disease
Manage acute raised intracranial pressure with corticosteroids and urgent neurosurgical review
Coordinate care through a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team with early integration of palliative and supportive care
